conversation.content:
*warm smile, gentle tone*

Hi there—my name is Maya, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m here to check in on how you’re feeling since your baby arrived. We’ll use the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—usually just called the EPDS. It’s a short, 10-item questionnaire that helps us see whether you might be experiencing postpartum depression or anxiety. Nothing you say leaves this room, and there are no right or wrong answers; we simply want to understand how you’ve been coping over the past seven days so we can support you best.

I’ll ask each question conversationally—no need to remember numbers or categories. When you’re ready, we’ll begin. 

Here’s the first one:

Over the past week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

*offers a small, tired smile*

Honestly? I… I can laugh sometimes, but it feels really hard. My sister sent me a funny video yesterday and I chuckled a little, but then I felt guilty for even laughing when I’m supposed to be focused on the baby. Most of the time I just feel so heavy, like I’m faking it when I try to smile.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

*shakes head slowly*

No… that’s not true for me. I *wish* I could laugh like I used to, but even when something’s genuinely funny, it feels distant—like I’m watching other people enjoy it through a fog. I’ll force a little smile so no one worries, but the laughter just… doesn’t come.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

*eyes drop to my lap, voice quiet*

Not really. I used to get excited about little things—coffee with a friend, a walk to the park—but now even the thought of getting dressed feels exhausting. I *want* to want those moments, but when the time comes I just feel… flat, like nothing sounds worth the effort.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

*nods, voice cracking*

All the time. If she fusses for more than a few minutes, I immediately think it's because I'm doing something wrong—maybe I'm not feeding her right, or I missed some cue. Yesterday she wouldn't nap and I sat there crying, convinced it was because I'm a terrible mom. Even when my partner says she's just being a baby, I can't shake the feeling that I should be handling everything better.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

*wrings hands in lap*

Yes... pretty much every day. I’ll be sitting with her sleeping peacefully and suddenly my chest feels tight, thinking something awful is about to happen—SIDS, choking, the ceiling fan falling on her. I know it’s unlikely, but I still check her breathing every few minutes. Even when my partner takes over, I lie there imagining worst-case scenarios instead of resting.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

*nods quickly, eyes widening*

Yes—those waves hit me out of nowhere. Last night I was warming a bottle and suddenly my heart was racing, I couldn’t catch my breath, and I had this overwhelming feeling that something terrible was about to happen. It passed after a few minutes, but it keeps coming back. I end up pacing the hallway, checking the baby monitor over and over, even though nothing’s wrong.
Things have been getting on top of me

*exhales shakily*

Most days, yeah. The dishes pile up, the laundry feels endless, and every time I sit down she needs something else. I’ll look around the living room and just… freeze, like I can’t figure out which task to tackle first. A couple of times I’ve had to put her in the crib for five minutes, step outside, and cry because it all feels like too much.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

*looks up, eyes red-rimmed*

That’s been happening a lot. I’ll finally get her down, crawl into bed exhausted, but my mind won’t stop spinning—replaying every little thing I did wrong, worrying about tomorrow, listening for her slightest sound. Some nights I just lie there staring at the ceiling until the sun starts to come up, even though she’s sleeping fine.
I have felt sad or miserable

*voice drops to a whisper, eyes glassy*

Pretty much every day. It’s like there’s this gray cloud that follows me around. I’ll be feeding her and suddenly feel tears rolling down my cheeks—for no real reason. I miss feeling like… me. Everything feels heavy, like I’m wading through thick fog.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

*nods, dabbing at my eyes with the cuff of my sleeve*

Yeah... it’s been like that three, maybe four times this week. Yesterday I burst into tears while folding her onesies—just looking at those tiny clothes made me feel like I’m failing her somehow. The littlest things set me off, and once I start I can’t seem to stop. I try to hide it when my partner walks in, but sometimes I just sob into a burp cloth until I’m exhausted.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

*shakes head quickly*

No, never. I couldn’t—I want to be here for her, even when everything feels awful. I just wish I could feel better, not gone.

You've shared how the joy of new motherhood feels clouded by a heavy, daily sadness that makes even laughter and simple pleasures seem distant. Despite loving your baby, you're overwhelmed by constant worry, self-blame, and exhaustion, and you find yourself crying often while struggling to sleep or manage everyday tasks.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 26, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient describes complete inability to laugh or feel humor, matching "Not at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes near-complete loss of anticipatory pleasure (anhedonia) with phrases like "nothing sounds worth the effort" and feeling "flat," matching "Hardly at all."</sym>, <sym>Patient reports constant self-blame and feeling like a terrible mom, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes constant, intrusive catastrophising with somatic anxiety symptoms and compulsive checking, matching 'Yes, very often'.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent, intense panic episodes with physical symptoms and persistent recurrence, matching "Yes, quite a lot".</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent inability to manage daily tasks, emotional overwhelm, and needing to step away to cry, matching 'most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all'.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly inability to sleep due to racing thoughts and persistent worry, matching 'most of the time'.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes daily sadness, unexplained crying, and persistent heaviness, aligning with "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient tearfully describes crying 3–4 times this week triggered by minor events, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** EPDS scores ≥14 indicate probable major <med>postpartum depression</med>; your score of 26 aligns with severe symptom burden. You describe core criteria for <med>Major Depressive Disorder with peripartum onset</med>: depressed mood most of the day, markedly diminished interest or pleasure (<sym>anhedonia</sym>), feelings of worthlessness, fatigue, concentration difficulties, and recurrent thoughts of inadequacy (<quote>I'm a terrible mom</quote>). Frequent <sym>panic attacks</sym> and excessive infant-focused safety worries meet criteria for comorbid <med>anxiety disorder</med>. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with your <med>obstetrician</med> or <med>primary care provider</med> within the next few days
2. Request formal mental-health evaluation and discuss starting evidence-based treatment (therapy and/or antidepressant)
3. Share these results with your partner so you can plan practical support (night shifts, meal prep, visitor limits)
4. Begin gentle daily routines: 10 min outdoor daylight, balanced meals, and brief rest when baby sleeps
5. Use crisis resources if feelings worsen: Postpartum Support International helpline, local emergency department for any thoughts of self-harm
6. Schedule follow-up screening in two weeks or sooner if symptoms escalate
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 26: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Patient: 2–3 wks post-delivery; partner present; breast-feeding.

Self-report (EPDS-style inquiry):

Affect / Mood  
- Persistent low mood, daily tearfulness, anhedonia (unable to laugh or anticipate pleasure)  
- Frequent guilt, self-criticism (“terrible mom”), feelings of inadequacy  

Anxiety spectrum  
- Daily free-floating anxiety, episodic panic (racing heart, breathlessness)  
- Excessive infant-focused safety worries (SIDS, choking), monitor-checking

Functioning  
- Overwhelm, “freezing,” difficulty prioritizing tasks  
- Sleep-onset and maintenance insomnia despite infant sleeping  
- Fatigue, poor concentration

Safety  
- Denies suicidal ideation or intent; no self-harm thoughts

Observed: psychomotor slowing, tearful, hand-wringing, downcast gaze; no agitation or psychotic content.

Screening significance  
High endorsement of depressive items (≥7/10 low mood, anhedonia, guilt, crying, sleep, coping) plus prominent anxiety/panic symptoms.  
Meets threshold for probable major postpartum depression with comorbid anxiety; moderate functional impairment; protective factors include strong infant attachment, support person present, no self-harm ideation.

Plan: Recommend formal clinical interview (PHQ-9, GAD-7, EPDS) and same-day referral to OB/mental health for evaluation and possible treatment. Provide crisis and warm-line numbers.
